y-m-24-01.title: If it worked for x=0 and x=1, does it work for every x?
y-m-24-01.topic: Calculating with letters: powers of the same letter and counterexamples
y-m-24-01.goal: Decide whether a few successful substitutions prove an expression for all numbers; make a counterexample and explain which values make both sides match by chance.
y-m-24-01.material: Sua says, "x²×x³ is x⁶!" (Reading: x squared times x cubed is x to the sixth.) Sua tried x=0 and both sides were 0, then x=1 and both sides were 1. Here x ranges from -5 to 5, including decimals.
y-m-24-01.thinking.0: Judge what it means when an example works
y-m-24-01.thinking.2: Explain cases that work by chance
y-m-24-01.prereq.0: Meaning of powers (for example, x³ is x multiplied by itself 3 times)
y-m-24-01.prereq.1: Find expression values by substituting negative numbers and decimals
y-m-24-01.s.s1.prompt: What can we conclude from Sua's check (both sides matched for x=0 and x=1)?
y-m-24-01.s.s1.hint.0: First compare 0 and 1, the numbers Sua chose, with other numbers.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.hint.1: To test Sua's statement, write 2 or 3 numbers you'd substitute for x.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.o.a: Both sides matched at x=0 and x=1, so it holds for every x.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.r.a: You turned two successes into 'it works for all numbers'. A few working examples do not mean all.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.o.b: Both sides matched for x=0 and x=1, but we don't know about other x yet.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.r.b: This judges only within the range of the examples checked. Choosing the next x matters.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.o.c: Both sides matched for x=0 and x=1, so it always holds for positive x.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.r.c: You narrowed 'all' to 'positive' but checked only one positive value, 1. Narrowing the range adds no evidence.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.o.d: Both sides matched for x=0 and x=1, so evidence shows Sua is wrong.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.r.d: You read the same result as evidence in the opposite direction. This check doesn't show it's wrong either.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.explain: We confirmed the values match only at 0 and 1. To find a counterexample, test x other than 0 and 1.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different x values where x²×x³ and x⁶ differ. (x is from -5 to 5)
y-m-24-01.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute 2 for x and calculate x²×x³ and x⁶ separately.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.hint.1: If a number gives the same value, try another. Negative numbers and decimals are okay too.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The values of x²×x³ and x⁶ differ. This is a counterexample to Sua's statement.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.fail.c2: For this x, both sides match. It does not disprove Sua's statement.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.explain: For example, x=2 gives x²×x³=4×8=32 but x⁶=64. At x=-1 they are -1 and 1; at x=0.5 they are 0.03125 and 0.015625. Only x=0 and x=1 make both sides match, so Sua happened to choose those two.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Tell Sua why both sides happened to match at x=0 and x=1, and why they differ for other values.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: You may use the x and calculation you found above.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write what happens to powers of 0 and 1.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: even if you take powers of 0 or 1, ... so ...
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain in your own words why using only 0 or 1 doesn't disprove the statement?
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you give at least one numeric x that disproves it?
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you distinguish 'matched by chance' from 'always match'?
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.model.0: 0 and 1 stay 0 and 1 when multiplied by themselves, so both sides happen to match. With x=2, x²×x³=32 but x⁶=64. Two successes don't prove it always works.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.model.1: They match only at x=0 and x=1, and differ elsewhere. For x=2, 4×8=32 while 2⁶=64. x²×x³ multiplies x five times; x⁶ multiplies it six times, so they differ.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: Explaining by how many times x is multiplied is also a good method.

y-m-24-02.title: Bike rental plans: which costs less for a longer ride?
y-m-24-02.topic: Using linear functions: compare two fare expressions
y-m-24-02.goal: Update your judgment as data arrives, then write a conditional notice based on when two linear fare expressions become equal.
y-m-24-02.material: A public bike station has two plans. A charges 1000원 base plus 150원 per minute; B charges 400원 base plus 200원 per minute. Time x is counted in 1-minute units, up to 60 minutes; fare is y원. Data will come one piece at a time.
y-m-24-02.thinking.0: Make a tentative judgment from partial data
y-m-24-02.thinking.1: Adjust confidence as new data arrives
y-m-24-02.prereq.0: Substitute numbers into a linear rule to find its value
y-m-24-02.prereq.1: Understand x as an amount in this situation, such as riding time in minutes
y-m-24-02.s.s1.prompt: Review each data piece and judge which plan costs less. It's okay to change your mind.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each data point, calculate and write the difference between A and B, and see how it changes.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.hint.1: If a cell doesn't fit your judgment, think of a condition that would explain it instead of changing your mind immediately.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Part of the fare table: at 0 minutes A=1000원 and B=400원; at 10 minutes A=2500원 and B=2400원.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: From just these 2 rows, which plan would you say costs less for longer rides?
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Predicting the shrinking difference as in c is fine, and waiting as in d is fine. But 'B stays cheaper' doesn't fit a difference shrinking from 600원 to 100원.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Even for longer rides, B stays cheaper.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You saw only that B was cheaper in both cells, not that the difference shrank from 600원 to 100원.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The longer you ride, the cheaper A stays than B.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You said the opposite even though the table has B cheaper. Can you find a reason in the table?
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: B is cheaper now, but A may become cheaper if you ride longer.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You carefully used the shrinking difference to predict what may happen later.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: There are only 2 cells, so we can't yet say which is cheaper.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This cautious judgment recognizes the small amount of data. You can still use the change in the difference already visible.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.info: New 20-minute fare: A is 4000원 and B is 4400원.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.after: B is cheaper at 0 and 10 minutes, but A at 20, so the switch lies between 10 and 20 minutes. If you first thought B would stay cheaper a bit longer, that part still holds.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Keep the judgment that B is always cheaper.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You kept your first judgment although new data doesn't fit; it can't explain the 20-minute value.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Somewhere between 10 and 20 minutes, the cheaper plan switches.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You noticed the order reversed and predicted the interval of the switch.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You used only the 20-minute cell. B was cheaper at 0 and 10 minutes.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The 20-minute data may be wrong, so keep the judgment so far.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Questioning data can be useful, but you have no reason to doubt it. Check the 20-minute fare with the expression.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.info: The shop notice gives fare rules: A: y=1000+150x, B: y=400+200x. Most users ride 8 to 15 minutes.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: What advice suits people who ride 8 to 15 minutes?
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.after: At 12 minutes both plans cost 2800원. B is cheaper under 12; A is cheaper over 12. Since 8 to 15 includes both sides of 12, one blanket recommendation is difficult.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Use 12 minutes as the cutoff: B costs less below it, A above it.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Substitute values into expressions to find when fares are equal, then split advice before and after.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: B's base fare is 600 won cheaper, so recommend B to everyone riding 8 to 15 minutes.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You looked only at base fare and missed how the per-minute difference grows over time.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: At 20 minutes A was 400 won cheaper, so recommend A to everyone riding 8 to 15 minutes.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You applied the 20-minute result directly to 8 to 15 without checking where the switch occurs.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The plans are never equal, so tell people the fare is the same whichever they choose.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You concluded without calculating whether they are ever equal. Substitute in the expressions to find when they match.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.reflect: With just two cells, you could first say only 'the difference is shrinking'. More data showed a switching point, and the expressions let you state it numerically. Say what data changed your judgment and how.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different riding times x (minutes) when plan A costs less than B. (x is a natural number from 1 to 60)
y-m-24-02.s.s2.hint.0: Put different values for x and write the A fare and B fare side by side.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.hint.1: Make the values bigger and check if A fit become cheaper, then B fit become cheaper again.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.ok.c1: Na e from 1 minute reach 60 minutes, in 1-minute units.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Make x one natural number from 1 reach 60, in 1-minute units.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The A fare cheap pass the B fare.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.fail.c2: At this time, A fare no cheap pass B. Calculate each fare separately, then compare dem.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.explain: At 13 minutes, A na 2950원 and B na 3000원. At 30 minutes, A na 5500원 and B na 6400원. From 13 reach 60 minutes, A dey cheaper every time; at 12 minutes dem equal, and under 12 minutes B dey cheaper.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.prompt: Write one or two sentences for the station notice. Talk which plan better for people wey ride 8 to 15 minutes, and put the time wey dem equal as number.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.hint.0: First find and write the time wey both fares equal, then write one line each to show which one cheap before and after that time.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.hint.1: Put 8 minutes and 15 minutes inside, compare both fares, and check if your sentence correct.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If you ride pass 12 minutes, ...
y-m-24-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You check am directly by putting values inside the expressions, to confirm say the equal time na 12 minutes?
y-m-24-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You think about exactly 12 minutes too, when dem equal?
y-m-24-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You divide the advice according to ride time, instead of recommending only one plan?
y-m-24-02.s.s3.model.0: If you ride under 12 minutes, plan B cheap pass; if you ride pass 12 minutes, plan A cheap pass. Exactly at 12 minutes, both na 2800원, same price.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.model.1: For people wey go ride 8 to 11 minutes, B cheap pass; for people wey go ride 13 to 15 minutes, A cheap pass. At 12 minutes dem equal, so any one fit do. If you no sabi how long you go ride, the difference small around 12 minutes, so B, wey get cheaper starting fare, go easier for pocket.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: E fit too to choose because the difference small.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.model.2: Before 12 minutes, plan B cheap pass; after 12 minutes, plan A cheap pass.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.modelNote.2: An answer wey use “before and after”

y-m-24-05.title: If you know only one point, e don determine the linear function?
y-m-24-05.topic: Linear function equation and graph: make equations wey meet conditions
y-m-24-05.goal: Understand by making equations yourself say if conditions no plenty, several equations fit work; when conditions add, the choices reduce; and some conditions impossible.
y-m-24-05.material: The graph of a linear function y=ax+b (a no be zero) na straight line. Jimin talk say, “If you only know say the graph pass through point (2, 5), the equation of this linear function don determine as only one!” (Read point (2, 5) as the point where y na 5 when x na 2. The x-intercept na the x-coordinate of the point where the graph meet the x-axis.)
y-m-24-05.thinking.1: Make different equations wey meet one condition
y-m-24-05.thinking.2: Explain why one impossible case no fit happen
y-m-24-05.prereq.0: Wetin a and b mean for the shape of graph y=ax+b (Grade 8 linear function topic level)
y-m-24-05.s.s1.prompt: Wetin you think about Jimin statement?
y-m-24-05.s.s1.hint.0: For a=1 and b=3, put x=2 inside the equation and check if e pass through point (2, 5).
y-m-24-05.s.s1.hint.1: Change a to other numbers, adjust b to match, and count how many equations wey pass through the point you fit get.
y-m-24-05.s.s1.o.a: E don determine. From the coordinates of one point, you fit find both a and b
y-m-24-05.s.s1.r.a: You think say one point tell you both values a and b. You no check how the two coordinate numbers relate to a and b in the equation.
y-m-24-05.s.s1.o.b: E no determine. No linear function at all pass through point (2, 5)
y-m-24-05.s.s1.r.b: You think say no linear function fit pass through the point at all. Try some a and b values and check if dem pass through the point.
y-m-24-05.s.s1.o.c: E don determine. The point coordinates na whole numbers, so a and b too na whole numbers and only one pair dey
y-m-24-05.s.s1.r.c: You think say if a point coordinates na whole numbers, a and b too must be whole numbers. Even when the coordinates na whole numbers, a and b no need to be.
y-m-24-05.s.s1.o.d: E no determine. Different pairs of a and b fit pass through the point
y-m-24-05.s.s1.r.d: Na the judgment wey check the relationship between a and b and see say different pairs dey.
y-m-24-05.s.s1.explain: To pass through point (2, 5), the equation must work when x=2 and y=5 enter, so e give only one relationship between a and b. a and b na two numbers but get one relationship, so different pairs dey. For example, (a, b)=(1, 3), (-1, 7), (5, -5) all pass through point (2, 5).
y-m-24-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different linear functions y=ax+b wey pass through point (2, 5) and get positive whole-number x-intercept. Enter suitable values for a and b. (You fit write only numbers wey you fit write as decimals.)
y-m-24-05.s.s2.hint.0: If the x-intercept fixed, the graph pass through two points, (x-intercept, 0) and (2, 5). Choose one x-intercept.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.hint.1: After you fix two points, calculate a and b, then check by putting x=2 if the point (2, 5) give 5.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.ok.c1: a no be 0, so na linear function.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.fail.c1: For am to be linear function, a must no be 0.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.fail.c2: When you put x=2, y no become 5, so e no pass through point (2, 5).
y-m-24-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The x-intercept na positive whole number.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The x-intercept (the x when y=0) no be positive whole number. Put y=0 and find x.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.explain: Call the x-intercept p. Then the graph pass through (p, 0) and (2, 5). y=5x-5 (x-intercept 1), y=-5x+15 (x-intercept 3), y=-2.5x+10 (x-intercept 4), and y=-x+7 (x-intercept 7) all meet the conditions. You fit make many more with fractional slopes too.
y-m-24-05.s.s3.prompt: Any linear function y=ax+b dey wey pass through point (2, 5) and get x-intercept 2? Answer “dey” or “no dey” and write the reason.
y-m-24-05.s.s3.hint.0: Rewrite “the x-intercept na 2” as the coordinates of point (□, 0).
y-m-24-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare that point x-coordinate with the x-coordinate of point (2, 5).
y-m-24-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: if x-intercept na 2, the graph must pass through point ..., so ...
y-m-24-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You first write wetin x-intercept 2 mean about the point wey the graph pass through?
y-m-24-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You use as reason say the same x go get two y values, or say 2a+b no fit be 0 and 5 at once?
y-m-24-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Your reason clear, using numbers 2, 0, and 5?
y-m-24-05.s.s3.model.0: No dey. If x-intercept na 2, e pass through (2, 0), but e must pass through (2, 5) too, so when x na 2, y go be two values, 0 and 5. For a linear function, each x must get exactly one y.
y-m-24-05.s.s3.model.1: Impossible. When you put x=2, 2a+b must be 0 and 5 at the same time, and that no fit happen. For the graph, e go be the vertical line x=2, and that no be linear function.
y-m-24-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: You fit explain am with the equation or the shape of the graph.

y-m-24-07.title: If dem share sweets, how many students dey?
y-m-24-07.topic: Apply linear inequalities: find possible cases from conditions wey give range
y-m-24-07.goal: Understand say when condition give one range, the answer no always be one fixed value; find all possible cases, then say what extra information we need to choose one.
y-m-24-07.material: You wan share sweets to x classmates. Total sweets na y. One way, give 4 sweets each and 3 remain. Another way, give 5 sweets each, where every student apart from the last get 5, while the last one get at least 1 and at most 4. (x na natural number at least 2.)
y-m-24-07.thinking.1: Find possible cases within a range condition
y-m-24-07.thinking.2: Suggest the extra information wey we need
y-m-24-07.prereq.0: Wetin linear inequality mean, and finding natural numbers wey meet conditions
y-m-24-07.s.s1.prompt: Do these conditions alone settle the number of students x as one value?
y-m-24-07.s.s1.hint.0: Put in one value for x, like 3, 4, or 5, and find how many sweets dey.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.hint.1: With that number of sweets, calculate how many the last student go get when we give 5 each.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.o.a: E no settle. The last student's share fit be from 1 to 4
y-m-24-07.s.s1.r.a: You see say the last student's share no be one number; dem give am as a range.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.o.b: E settle as one. 4x+3 and 5x must equal, so x get only one value
y-m-24-07.s.s1.r.b: You set both amounts equal like a “short” problem. Here the last student no get full 5, so we no fit say e equal 5x.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.o.c: We no fit know, because we no know total number of sweets
y-m-24-07.s.s1.r.c: You think say not knowing the sweet total na the problem. The number of sweets connect to x through the expression for giving 4 each.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.o.d: E no settle. Any number of students fit work, no matter how many sweets dey
y-m-24-07.s.s1.r.d: You think say the conditions hardly limit the students. You no work out how each condition limit x.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.explain: Between number of students and number of sweets, 2 conditions dey: “give 4 each, 3 remain” and “last student get 1 to 4”. Work out directly if one or several x values fit these conditions. Next, list possible cases and check dem.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different pairs (number of students x, number of sweets y) wey meet both conditions. (If you give 4 each, 3 remain; if you give 5 each, the last student get at least 1 and at most 4.)
y-m-24-07.s.s2.hint.0: Fix number of students x, find number of sweets y, then calculate how many sweets remain after giving 5 each to x-1 students.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.hint.1: Change x one by one, put the leftover numbers in a table, and check the range wey meet the condition.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of students na natural number at least 2.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be natural number at least 2.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.fail.c2: This no match the condition say 3 sweets remain after giving 4 each. Add the 3 leftover to the 4 sweets wey you give x students.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.ok.c3: Even when you give 5 each, the last student get at least 1 and at most 4.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.fail.c3: When you give 5 each, the last student's sweets no dey between 1 and 4. Check how many remain after giving 5 each to (x-1) students.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.explain: The possible cases na (4, 19), (5, 23), (6, 27), (7, 31), 4 altogether. For example, with 6 students, sweets dey 27; if you give 5 each to 5 students, na 25 sweets, and the last student go get 2. With 3 students the last student go still get 5, and with 8 students the last student go get 0, so dem no meet the conditions.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.prompt: Wetin one extra information fit we give to settle the number of students as exactly one value? Write the information as number and write the number of students for that case too.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.hint.0: Put the number of sweets and the last student's share side by side for the 4 possible cases.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.hint.1: Find the value in the table wey separate the 4 cases.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If you know the last student get ... sweets, then students dey ...
y-m-24-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You check say the information you choose leave just one among the 4 possible cases?
y-m-24-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You calculate the number of students from your information and check say e correct?
y-m-24-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You think of other information wey fit too settle the number as one?
y-m-24-07.s.s3.model.0: If you tell us the last student get 3 sweets, the number of students settle as 5.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.model.1: If you tell us total sweets na 27, remove the 3 leftover from giving 4 each, then divide the remaining 24 sweets by 4; the number of students na 6.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: The method wey give the total number of sweets too work.

y-m-24-04.title: The drink number solution: where e start to go wrong?
y-m-24-04.topic: Apply linear inequalities: understand “less than” and “at most”
y-m-24-04.goal: For an inequality word problem solution, find the line wey no match the sentence meaning, and explain with number check how the answer change when the condition wording change.
y-m-24-04.material: Hyeonu wan buy drinks for school event. One drink bottle cost 900원, and cooler box cost 3000원, paid once. Teacher talk say, “Spend under 12000원.” Hyeonu call the number of drinks wey e buy x and write the solution. (x na natural number. Read 900x as “nine hundred x”, < mean less than, and ≤ mean less than or equal to.)
y-m-24-04.thinking.1: Compare answers based on how the condition dey worded
y-m-24-04.thinking.2: Check corrected solution with number calculation
y-m-24-04.prereq.0: Show situation with linear inequality, and wetin signs < and ≤ mean
y-m-24-04.prereq.1: Read the answer as whole number for natural-number counting problems
y-m-24-04.s.s1.prompt: Pick the first line in Hyeonu solution wey no match the sentence meaning.
y-m-24-04.s.s1.hint.0: Check one by one if each line mean the same thing as the line before am.
y-m-24-04.s.s1.hint.1: Actually buy the number of bottles wey the conclusion talk, calculate the money spent, and check if e match the sentence.
y-m-24-04.s.s1.line.0: If e buy x drink bottles, the money e spend na 900x+3000 (원).

y-m-24-03.title: The three friends write simultaneous equations: which one match this problem?

y-m-24-03.material: 10 adults and children enter one amusement park. Adult ticket na 3000원 per person and child ticket na 2000원 per person, and dem pay 24000원 altogether. For 나, 3 and 2 in 3x+2y use thousand 원 units, but 24000 use 원, so e no match. For 라, the adult and child fares swap, so x=6 and y=4 come out, reversing the number of adults and children.

y-m-24-06.title: The sum of four calendar squares: how correct Jiyun statement be?
y-m-24-06.topic: Expressions with letters: explain the sum of numbers on a calendar
y-m-24-06.goal: Use new information to revise one rule made from a few examples, set up an expression with letters to check the condition wey make the rule work, then make examples for another condition in the same way.
y-m-24-06.material: Calendar get 7 squares in one row (Sun to Sat). This month get 31 days and the 1st na Sunday. So 1st to 7th dey first row, and 8th to 14th dey second row. If you pick one 2×2 block of squares (2 squares across and 2 down), you get four numbers. Jiyun talk say, “If you add the four numbers in a 2×2 block, the answer always be multiple of 8!”
